summary: Explains how a SIP user agent obtains and uses a Globally Routable User Agent URI (GRUU), an address that anyone can use to reach that one specific device instance rather than just the person.

plainLanguage.summary: A person may have several phones. A GRUU is like the exact phone's own number, so calls reach that single phone.

subtitle: A SIP address that reaches one specific device, usable by anyone on the Internet.

tldr.problem: A SIP address of record points to a whole group of devices, yet features like call transfer need a URI that reaches exactly one device instance and works from anywhere. IP addresses and hostnames fail behind NATs and firewalls.
tldr.mechanism: A device registers with an instance ID, and the registrar returns a public GRUU and a temporary GRUU. Both carry the gr URI parameter and route to a proxy in the domain, which maps the GRUU to the right registered contact.
tldr.outcome: A user agent can put a GRUU in its Contact header field and hand it to peers, who can then reach that exact device. It is a Proposed Standard.

facts.label: URI parameter
facts.value: gr, with or without a value

today: RFC 5627 is a Proposed Standard from October 2009, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on RFC 3261 and RFC 5626.

sections.title: The Problem a GRUU Solves
sections.content:
In SIP the basic unit of reference is the Address of Record (AOR), but one user can have many user agents (handsets, softphones, voicemail) behind the same AOR. Some uses need an identifier for a single user agent instead.

The RFC's example is a blind transfer. User A talks to user B and sends a REFER to user C, with a Refer-To URI that identifies B's user agent. If A gives C only B's AOR, the call might reach B's voicemail instead of B's current handset. B therefore provides an instance-specific URI in its Contact header field. Because B does not know who will use it, the URI has to work for anyone.

Clients that use explicit IP addresses in Contact interact poorly with NATs and firewalls, hostnames have proven problematic, and many clients have no hostname at all. The Globally Routable UA URI (GRUU) fills this gap.
sections.plainLanguage: Calling a family's shared phone number might ring any phone in the house. Sometimes you need the number of one particular phone, and it has to work from anywhere in the world.

sections.title: What a GRUU Looks Like
sections.content:
A GRUU is a SIP URI with two properties: it routes to a specific user agent instance, and any user agent on the Internet can dereference it. GRUUs are issued by SIP domains and always route back to a proxy in that domain, which maps the GRUU to the contact of the instance. Every GRUU contains the gr URI parameter, with or without a value.

There are two kinds. A public GRUU is the AOR plus a gr parameter with a value chosen by the registrar, for example sip:alice@example.com;gr=kjh29x97us97d. Removing gr yields the AOR. A temporary GRUU hides the AOR so a recipient cannot readily determine it, for example sip:asd887f9dfkk76690@example.com;gr. It is often built as a cryptographically protected stateless value to avoid excess state in the registrar.
sections.plainLanguage: A public GRUU is a phone number that clearly shows whose phone it is. A temporary GRUU is a code number that reaches the phone without saying whose it is.

sections.title: Obtaining GRUUs by Registering
sections.content:
A user agent obtains a GRUU in one of three ways: from its REGISTER transaction, by constructing a self-made GRUU from its own IP address or hostname (only when it knows it is globally reachable), or by a locally specified administrative mechanism.

In a REGISTER request the UA MUST include a Supported header field with the gruu option tag. For each contact it MUST include the +sip.instance parameter holding its instance ID (from RFC 5626). The registrar then returns pub-gruu and temp-gruu Contact parameters in the 2xx response. A UA MUST be ready for either, both or neither to appear, and MUST treat the user and host parts of a GRUU opaquely.

On each refresh the registrar returns the same public GRUU but creates a new temporary GRUU. Earlier temporary GRUUs stay valid while a contact with that instance ID remains registered and the UA keeps the same Call-ID in its REGISTER requests. Changing the Call-ID invalidates all previous temporary GRUUs, so a UA that wants them to survive MUST keep the same Call-ID. When the last contact for the instance expires, all temporary GRUUs are invalidated.
sections.plainLanguage: The phone tells the phone company "this is me, phone number 123". The company hands back a name-tag number and some throwaway numbers, and the throwaways stop working if the phone starts a new conversation with a new code.

sections.title: Using and Rendering GRUUs
sections.content:
A UA SHOULD use one of its GRUUs in the Contact header field of dialog-forming and target refresh requests and responses, such as INVITE, SUBSCRIBE, NOTIFY, REFER and UPDATE. It MUST have an active registration before using a registered GRUU, and MUST NOT reuse one learned from a lapsed registration. It MAY use the public GRUU or a temporary one, and SHOULD use a temporary GRUU for anonymous requests as described in RFC 3323. When it has several AORs, the GRUU SHOULD match the AOR used for the request.

A UA sending a request to a GRUU knows it will reach a specific instance, and SHOULD NOT apply non-standard URI-handling workarounds to a contact URI with gr. Sending to the AOR with an Accept-Contact preference for an instance is not equivalent, because caller preferences are only preferences. When showing a GRUU to a person, the gr parameter is RECOMMENDED to be removed, which gives the AOR for a public GRUU.
sections.plainLanguage: When a phone starts or answers a call, it tells the other side "call me back at my own personal number." If it does not want to be recognized, it uses a throwaway number.

sections.title: What the Registrar Does
sections.content:
If a REGISTER contact has +sip.instance and a non-zero expiration, the registrar applies the GRUU rules. It MUST reject with 403 a contact that is equivalent to the AOR, is a GRUU for that AOR, or is not a SIP URI. If no valid public GRUU exists for the AOR and instance ID, the registrar SHOULD construct one by adding gr with a value to the AOR. It ignores any pub-gruu or temp-gruu the UA supplies, since a UA cannot suggest GRUUs.

If the Call-ID differs from the most recently registered contact for the same AOR and instance ID, the registrar MUST invalidate all earlier temporary GRUUs, and requests to them then get a 404. It SHOULD create a new temporary GRUU. The construction algorithm MUST make a collision vanishingly unlikely and MUST make it computationally infeasible to tell whether two GRUUs belong to the same AOR or instance.

Each GRUU is tied to one AOR and one instance ID, and resolves only to contacts with that instance ID. A public GRUU stays valid as long as the AOR does; after its contacts expire it SHOULD still be treated as valid and requests return 480 (Temporarily Unavailable). The GRUU's domain part MUST resolve to a public Internet address and requests MUST route to an authoritative proxy.
sections.plainLanguage: The phone company keeps a list that ties each personal number to one phone. Old throwaway numbers get cancelled when the phone restarts its conversation with a new code.

sections.title: How Proxies Route to a GRUU
sections.content:
An authoritative proxy that sees a Request-URI with gr that does not match a currently valid GRUU SHOULD answer 404. If it matches, the proxy looks it up in the location service like an AOR, keeping gr only for the lookup, and rewrites the Request-URI to the registered contact. With no bound contacts it MUST return 480. With several, it follows the reg-id rules of RFC 5626 or, otherwise, MUST pick the most recently refreshed contact, retrying the next one on 408 or 430.

Screening is RECOMMENDED for out-of-dialog requests, but call forwarding SHOULD NOT be applied and the request SHOULD NOT be redirected, because a GRUU targets one instance. Record-routing rules in Section 6.2 require an authoritative proxy to record-route in specified cases, which avoids request spirals.
sections.plainLanguage: The phone company's switchboard looks up the personal number, finds the one phone behind it, and connects the call there without forwarding it elsewhere.

sections.title: Example Call Flow
sections.content:
The RFC's example has a callee register with Supported: gruu and an instance ID. The 200 OK carries both a pub-gruu and a temp-gruu. The callee then answers an INVITE using its public GRUU in the Contact. Later the caller sends a SUBSCRIBE directly to that GRUU, and the proxy translates it into the callee's registered contact.

Finally the callee's machine crashes and comes back with a new IP address, 192.0.2.2, and re-registers with the same instance ID. The registrar keeps the same public GRUU, creates a second temporary GRUU, and returns both contacts. The UA need not remove the stale contact, because the targeting rules deliver requests to the most recent one.
sections.plainLanguage: A phone gets a personal number, someone uses it during a call to reach that phone only, and when the phone restarts with a new address, the same number still works.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
A tampered GRUU in a REGISTER response could deny service to the UA, so a UA is RECOMMENDED to use the SIPS URI scheme when registering. Public GRUU guessing is possible, which is why screening features SHOULD apply to requests sent to a GRUU, so a GRUU is not a back door for someone the user has blocked.

A malicious correspondent could try to use a victim's GRUU in the Contact of a SUBSCRIBE to a presence server, steering traffic at the victim. The spec mitigates this by requiring proxies to check that the GRUU in the Contact matches the authenticated identity of the sender. This needs an outbound proxy, which SIP does not require, though the RFC notes that nearly all deployments use one.

For privacy, temporary GRUUs hide the AOR and instance ID. Reusing one temporary GRUU lets correspondents link calls to one UA, while using a different one per call does not. IP addresses in SDP can still reveal location and ISP absent network privacy, and a correspondent can always see the SIP service provider.
sections.plainLanguage: The throwaway numbers keep your real identity hidden. But if you give the same throwaway number to everyone, they can tell it is the same phone calling.
